messages.content: I want to develop offline policy improvement certificates that remain valid under bounded hidden confounding, without requiring full action coverage. Can we make that goal precise?

The aim is to assess a proposed policy using offline information and issue a certificate about its gain relative to the behavior policy. The certificate must account for hidden confounding up to a stated bound, and its validity must not depend on full action coverage. There are two required outcomes: the certificates must attain at least 95% coverage of the true policy gains under that confounding bound, and they must certify strictly positive gains over the behavior policy in a nontrivial, explicitly characterized regime.
What exactly is the gain being discussed?

It is the proposed policy's gain over the behavior policy. A strictly positive gain means improvement relative to that baseline, rather than merely matching it. The goal concerns certificates for that comparison; it does not specify a particular policy class, data set, or formula for measuring the gain.
Does the 95% requirement mean that at least 95% of policies must improve?

No. It is a coverage requirement for the true policy gains, not a claim about the fraction of policies that improve. Whatever form the certificate takes, it must cover the true gain at least 95% of the time under the stated confounding bound. Coverage and improvement are separate requirements: a certificate could have the required coverage yet be too inconclusive to establish a positive gain.
And is 95% coverage meant to make each individual certificate certain?

No. A coverage guarantee does not turn an individual certificate into an absolute guarantee that cannot fail. It specifies the required reliability of the certificate procedure with respect to the true gain. The stated confounding bound is part of the conditions under which that reliability must hold.
How does hidden confounding change the claim?

The certificate cannot simply rely on an assumption that there is no hidden confounding. It must remain valid when hidden confounding is present within the stated bound. The goal does not give the numerical value or the formal definition of that bound, so those details should not be filled in here. The essential qualification is that the at-least-95% coverage claim is made under the bound, not for unrestricted hidden confounding.
What does it mean not to require full action coverage?

Full action coverage would demand complete coverage of the relevant actions in the offline information. The goal explicitly rules out making that a prerequisite for valid certificates. That is different from claiming that a certificate can establish improvement in every setting with missing action coverage. The intended validity must avoid the full-coverage requirement, while any limitations on when a positive gain can be certified need to be stated honestly.
So the absence of full action coverage is not itself a positive-gain result?

Right. Removing a full-action-coverage requirement addresses an assumption behind validity; it does not automatically establish improvement. The other requirement is substantive: there must be a nontrivial regime, described explicitly, in which the certificates actually certify gains that are strictly greater than zero relative to the behavior policy.
Why emphasize strictly positive instead of nonnegative?

Because a certificate that only supports a gain of zero or more could leave open the possibility of no improvement at all. Strict positivity rules out zero in the improvement claim. In the familiar case of a certified lower bound on gain, for example, that would require the lower bound itself to be above zero. That is an illustration of the distinction, not a prescribed form for these certificates.
What work is the phrase “nontrivial, explicitly characterized regime” doing?

It prevents the positive-gain requirement from being satisfied by an empty, purely formal, or unexplained case. The regime where strict improvement can be certified must have conditions that can be stated clearly, and it must be meaningful rather than vacuous. The goal does not yet identify those conditions, so it would be premature to name a specific regime as though it had been established.
Could the method meet the coverage target while never certifying a positive gain?

That would satisfy only one part of the goal. A procedure can be reliably cautious and still be uninformative about improvement. Here, the at-least-95% coverage requirement and the ability to certify strictly positive gains in a nontrivial, explicitly characterized regime must both be met.
Conversely, what if it often declares improvement but its certificates do not cover the true gains at least 95% of the time?

That would not meet the goal either. Frequent declarations of improvement cannot substitute for the stated coverage requirement under bounded hidden confounding. The positive conclusions must come from certificates with the required validity, rather than from an improvement claim assessed separately from that validity.
Is the behavior policy only a point of reference, or is it also part of the certification requirement?

It is the explicit comparison baseline. The positive-gain requirement is not merely to say that a proposed policy has some favorable value in isolation; it is to certify a strictly positive gain over the behavior policy. Keeping that baseline in the statement makes clear what the certified improvement is relative to.
Can we promise the same positive conclusion whenever hidden confounding stays within the bound?

Not from this goal alone. Staying within the stated bound is part of the validity condition for coverage, but the goal calls for positive-gain certification in a nontrivial, explicitly characterized regime—not in every possible case covered by the bound. In some cases, a valid certificate could remain inconclusive about whether the gain is strictly positive.
How would you state the goal without quietly adding an algorithm or an experiment?

Develop offline certificates for policy gains relative to the behavior policy that remain valid under a stated bound on hidden confounding without requiring full action coverage. Require at least 95% coverage of the true policy gains under that bound, and require the certificates to establish strictly positive gains over the behavior policy in a nontrivial regime whose conditions are explicitly characterized. That states the intended guarantees without claiming a particular construction or that the guarantees have already been demonstrated.
So the two requirements should be read together, rather than treating 95% as the amount of improvement?

Yes. At least 95% is the coverage target for true gains under the stated confounding bound; it is not a minimum percentage improvement. Strictly positive describes the direction of the gain over the behavior policy, and the nontrivial, explicitly characterized regime says where that positive conclusion must be attainable. The certificates need to satisfy both requirements without making full action coverage a prerequisite.
For the offline improvement goal, could we use sample-split Γ-odds sensitivity bounds to certify supported-action policy switches when their 95% lower gain bound exceeds zero?

That is a concrete proposal for pursuing the goal. It focuses on policy switches involving supported actions, evaluates their gain relative to the behavior policy under a Γ-odds bound on hidden confounding, and calls a switch an improvement only when its 95% lower gain bound is strictly above zero. The sample split is part of the proposed certification approach. Those ingredients describe what to try; they do not, by themselves, establish the required coverage or show that a positive certificate is attainable in a nontrivial regime.
What is the role of Γ here?

Γ denotes the bound used by the odds-based sensitivity analysis for hidden confounding. The proposed lower gain bound is meant to account for confounding allowed by that bound. No numerical value of Γ or detailed sensitivity model has been specified here, so the proposal should be understood as conditional on a stated Γ-odds bound, not as protection against arbitrary hidden confounding.
Why call it a sensitivity bound rather than just a confidence bound?

The two qualifications address different uncertainties. The Γ-odds sensitivity component concerns how hidden confounding within the stated bound could affect the assessed gain. The 95% lower-bound component concerns the statistical coverage intended for the gain bound. Combining them is the proposal; demonstrating that the resulting lower bound has the required coverage under the confounding bound remains necessary.
What exactly triggers a certificate of improvement?

For a supported-action policy switch, the proposed decision rule is strict: issue a positive-gain certificate when its 95% lower gain bound exceeds zero. A lower bound equal to zero does not pass that rule, nor does one below zero. The comparison is the gain over the behavior policy.
Does a lower bound at zero mean the switch is harmful?

No. It means this rule does not certify a strictly positive gain. The true gain might be positive, zero, or negative while a lower bound fails to exceed zero. Failure to certify improvement should not be recast as a finding of harm.
Why restrict the proposal to supported-action switches?

It gives the proposal a way to focus on switches for which the relevant actions have support, without demanding full action coverage across all actions. That is a narrower scope for certification, not a claim that unsupported switches can be assessed in the same way. The precise meaning of support and the set of eligible switches have not been specified in this node.
Is that the same as assuming full action coverage after all?

No. Full action coverage would make coverage of all relevant actions a general prerequisite. This proposal instead targets policy switches involving supported actions. Its scope can therefore be narrower than the full action space. That distinction does not automatically guarantee a useful certificate; it says which switches the proposed approach seeks to certify.
What does sample-split contribute conceptually?

Sample splitting separates uses of offline information so that a choice informed by one portion need not be treated as though it were fixed independently of that same information when assessed on another portion. In this proposal, it is part of how the sensitivity-based gain certificate would be constructed. The node does not prescribe a split ratio or an exact allocation of tasks to the portions.
Are we claiming sample splitting alone ensures the 95% coverage target?

No. Sample splitting is a proposed ingredient, not a proof of coverage. To meet the goal, the resulting certificates would still need to attain at least 95% coverage of the true policy gains under the stated confounding bound. Calling an output a “95% lower gain bound” expresses its intended coverage level; its validity must be justified under the conditions actually used.
How do the 95% lower bound and the earlier at-least-95% coverage requirement fit together?

The proposal uses a 95% lower gain bound as the basis for its improvement decision. If that bound has its claimed one-sided coverage for the true gain under the stated Γ-odds bound, it addresses the goal's at-least-95% coverage requirement in lower-bound form. The implication depends on establishing that coverage; the decision rule alone cannot supply it.
Could we simply declare that any bound above zero proves improvement despite hidden confounding?

Only with the appropriate qualification. If the 95% lower gain bound is valid under the stated Γ-odds sensitivity model and it exceeds zero, it supports a certificate of strictly positive gain over the behavior policy at the stated coverage level. The claim remains conditional on the confounding bound and the bound's statistical validity. It is not an unconditional claim about all possible hidden confounding.
Does the proposal say which switches will have a bound above zero?

No. It states a criterion for certifying a supported-action switch, not a result that any particular switch meets it. The broader goal requires positive certificates in a nontrivial, explicitly characterized regime. This proposal points to the form such certificates could take, but it does not yet characterize that regime or demonstrate that the lower bound exceeds zero within it.
Suppose a supported-action switch has an estimated gain that looks positive, but its 95% lower gain bound does not exceed zero. Would it qualify?

No. Under the proposed rule, a favorable point estimate would not suffice. The 95% lower gain bound itself must be strictly greater than zero, after accounting for the stated Γ-odds sensitivity bound. That is what makes the proposed positive conclusion a certificate rather than merely an observed positive estimate.
And a switch involving an unsupported action cannot be certified by this particular proposal just because its apparent gain is large?

Correct. The proposal is specifically for supported-action policy switches. An apparent gain does not remove that scope condition or substitute for a valid 95% lower gain bound above zero. This says what the proposed certificate covers, without drawing a conclusion about the true gain of an unsupported switch.
Can you put the proposed rule into one sentence without making it sound like an established result?

Propose using sample-split Γ-odds sensitivity bounds to assess supported-action policy switches, and certify a switch's gain over the behavior policy as strictly positive when its valid 95% lower gain bound exceeds zero. Establishing coverage under the stated confounding bound and identifying a nontrivial regime where that happens remain requirements, not completed results.
What overlap and reward-gap conditions would yield positive Γ-robust lower gain bounds for supported-action switches?

At a conceptual level, the switched-to actions need enough overlap with the offline data to support a meaningful lower gain bound, and the reward advantage of switching needs to remain positive after accounting for both uncertainty and the hidden confounding allowed by Γ. Those are two different conditions: overlap makes the comparison assessable, while a sufficiently large reward gap makes a positive conclusion possible. The question does not yet specify quantitative thresholds for either.
Does “supported action” already settle the overlap question?

Not completely. Support identifies actions within the proposal’s scope, but it does not by itself say how informative the available evidence is for a particular switch. A supported action could still leave a lower bound too uncertain to exceed zero. An explicit positive-gain regime would need to say what degree of overlap is sufficient for the intended bound, rather than treating support as an automatic certificate.
How is that different from requiring full action coverage?

The overlap condition can be local to the actions involved in the switches being assessed. It need not require every action to be covered. The aim is to characterize when a supported-action switch can receive a valid and informative certificate, while retaining the proposal’s distinction between support for those switches and full action coverage.
What should the reward gap be measured against?

Against the behavior-policy comparison relevant to the proposed switch. The question is whether making that switch yields a gain over the behavior policy, not whether the switched-to action has a favorable reward in isolation. A reward-gap condition would therefore need to be tied to that gain comparison.
Would any positive reward gap be enough?

Not necessarily. A gap can be positive while too small to survive the Γ-robust adjustment or the uncertainty reflected in a 95% lower gain bound. To certify improvement under the proposed rule, the resulting lower bound—not just an unadjusted or estimated gap—must exceed zero.
Can you explain how Γ enters the reward-gap condition without choosing a numerical value for it?

The condition must be strong enough that the gain remains certifiably positive when hidden confounding is allowed within the stated Γ-odds bound. Γ defines the sensitivity qualification under which the lower bound is intended to hold. Without a specified value of Γ and a precise bound construction, we cannot state a numerical minimum reward gap; we can only say that the gap must withstand the confounding allowance embodied in the Γ-robust lower bound.
Is stronger overlap a substitute for a reward gap?

No. Better overlap may make a gain comparison more informative, but it does not create a positive gain if the comparison offers no advantage. Conversely, a promising reward gap may be difficult to certify if overlap is insufficient to make the lower bound informative. A positive Γ-robust lower gain bound depends on both aspects working together.
What would an explicitly characterized regime look like in terms of this question?

It would state conditions on overlap for the actions involved in a switch and conditions on the reward gap relative to the behavior policy that are sufficient for the Γ-robust 95% lower gain bound to exceed zero. It would also make clear the confounding bound under which that conclusion is asserted. That describes what needs to be characterized; it does not supply or establish a particular set of thresholds.
Could the reward-gap condition just say, “the 95% lower bound is positive”?

That would restate the certification rule rather than explain when it can succeed. The useful question is what underlying overlap and reward-gap conditions lead to a lower bound above zero. A characterization should make those conditions understandable without assuming the desired positive certificate as a premise.
Suppose the reward advantage appears large, but the Γ-robust lower gain bound crosses zero. How should I describe that case?

As a switch for which this rule does not certify a strictly positive gain. An apparent advantage is not enough if the lower bound fails to exceed zero. That result would not, on its own, establish that the switch has no gain; it would say that a positive gain has not been certified under the stated bound and coverage criterion.
And if overlap is present but the reward gap is small?

Overlap alone would not make the lower bound positive. The reward gap would still have to be large enough, in the relevant comparison, for the Γ-robust 95% lower gain bound to clear zero. Whether a particular gap suffices depends on the formal bound and its uncertainty, which are not specified in the question.
Should the overlap condition cover all possible policy switches, or only the ones we want to certify?

The question concerns supported-action switches, so an overlap condition aimed at those switches is the pertinent one. Demanding overlap for every possible switch would move toward a broader coverage requirement than the proposal calls for. The condition should still be explicit enough to identify which switches it applies to.
Can I say that sufficient overlap guarantees a positive lower gain bound if the switch has a positive estimated reward gap?

That would be too strong as stated. An estimated positive gap can coexist with a lower bound at or below zero. The relevant gap condition must account for what the Γ-robust analysis and the 95% lower-bound uncertainty can remove from the apparent advantage. Sufficient overlap helps make that assessment possible; it does not turn every positive estimate into a positive certificate.
So is the question asking for a joint condition rather than two independent checkboxes?

Yes. It asks how much overlap is needed for a supported-action switch to be assessed informatively and how large its reward gap must be for the Γ-robust lower gain bound to remain above zero. The conditions may need to be expressed together, because the informativeness of the lower bound affects how large an advantage can be certified. No specific quantitative relationship has been given yet.
How would you state the open question precisely, without pretending we already know its answer?

For supported-action policy switches, identify explicit overlap and reward-gap conditions, relative to the behavior policy and under a stated Γ-odds hidden-confounding bound, that make the valid 95% lower gain bound strictly positive. The task is to find and justify those conditions; the question itself does not claim that a particular overlap threshold or reward gap has already been shown sufficient.

Here is a hypothesis about when the proposed lower gain bounds become positive: in eight-stratum binary bandits with unit-bounded rewards, Γ≤1.25, switched-action propensity≥0.2, switch-mass≥0.1, and observed gap≥0.3 yield positive 95% bounds at n≥20,000. Is that a precise way to frame it?

Yes, as a hypothesis. It gives a concrete candidate regime for positive 95% lower gain bounds for supported-action switches. The conditions are joint: an eight-stratum binary bandit setting with unit-bounded rewards, Γ at most 1.25, switched-action propensity at least 0.2, switch-mass at least 0.1, an observed gap of at least 0.3, and sample size n of at least 20,000. The statement proposes that the bounds are positive under those conditions; it does not report that this has been demonstrated.
Why stress that the conditions are joint?

Because the hypothesis does not say that propensity≥0.2, switch-mass≥0.1, or observed gap≥0.3 is sufficient on its own. It proposes positivity when all the stated setting and threshold conditions hold together. It also makes no claim about what happens when one of them fails.
Is Γ≤1.25 an estimate of the actual hidden confounding?

Not as stated. Γ≤1.25 is the confounding-bound condition in the hypothesis. The proposed positive bound would be assessed under that Γ-odds sensitivity allowance. The hypothesis does not establish the actual amount of hidden confounding or claim validity beyond the stated bound.
How should I read switched-action propensity≥0.2?

It is the proposed overlap threshold for the action involved in the switch: the switched-action propensity must be at least 0.2. That makes the overlap requirement numerical rather than simply saying the action is supported. The hypothesis does not spell out a more detailed definition of that propensity, so I would not add one to the claim.
And what is switch-mass≥0.1 adding if we already have the propensity threshold?

It is a separate condition on the mass of the switch. The propensity threshold concerns overlap for the switched action; the switch-mass threshold concerns how much mass the switch has. Both appear in the proposed regime, and the hypothesis does not say that either threshold can replace the other.
Does observed gap≥0.3 mean we already know the true policy gain is at least 0.3?

No. The threshold is explicitly for an observed gap. It should not be silently converted into a claim about the true gain, or about a Γ-robust lower gain bound of 0.3. The hypothesis is that, when this observed-gap threshold holds along with the other conditions, the resulting 95% lower bound is positive—not that the lower bound itself equals or exceeds 0.3.
Why might a gap of 0.3 still need the other conditions before a positive certificate can be expected?

An observed gap is only one input to the proposed certificate. The Γ-robust lower gain bound must also account for the stated hidden-confounding allowance and the uncertainty relevant to a 95% lower bound. The overlap, switch-mass, reward-boundedness, setting, and sample-size conditions are all part of the hypothesized regime in which the observed gap is expected to suffice. That is the proposed relationship, not an established calculation.
Is n≥20,000 meant as a sample-size threshold rather than a number of switches?

The notation n≥20,000 states a sample-size threshold. The hypothesis does not separately specify a count of switches, observations per stratum, or observations per action. Those quantities should not be inferred from n or from the switch-mass and propensity thresholds without further definitions.
What exactly does “unit-bounded rewards” contribute to the statement?

It restricts the reward scale in the hypothesized setting. It is part of the conditions under which positivity is proposed, so dropping it would broaden the claim. The statement does not give a more specific reward distribution, and it does not by itself establish that the 95% bound is positive.
Does “eight-stratum binary bandits” mean the same thresholds are claimed for arbitrary offline policy problems?

No. The hypothesis is explicitly confined to eight-stratum binary bandits with the other listed conditions. It should not be generalized to other numbers of strata or different settings on the strength of this statement alone.
If Γ is exactly 1.25, propensity is exactly 0.2, switch-mass is exactly 0.1, observed gap is exactly 0.3, and n is exactly 20,000, are those included?

Yes. The non-strict inequalities include their boundary values: Γ≤1.25, and each of switched-action propensity≥0.2, switch-mass≥0.1, observed gap≥0.3, and n≥20,000 includes equality. The proposed conclusion is different: the 95% lower gain bound must be strictly positive, rather than merely equal to zero.
Is the hypothesis claiming that every switch meeting those thresholds has already been certified?

No. It posits that the joint conditions yield positive 95% bounds. Until that assertion is justified, it remains a hypothesis about when certification should be possible, not a report of certificates already obtained for particular switches.
Could I describe it as a proposed answer to the overlap-and-reward-gap question?

Yes. It proposes explicit numerical conditions involving switched-action propensity and switch-mass for the switch, and an observed-gap threshold, within a specified bandit setting and Γ bound. Its proposed answer is conditional: at n≥20,000, those joint conditions are hypothesized to yield positive 95% lower gain bounds. Whether they actually suffice remains to be established.
If the lower bound were zero despite all those conditions, how would that relate to this statement?

A bound equal to zero would not be positive, so it would not satisfy the conclusion predicted by the hypothesis. How to interpret such a case would depend on whether the stated conditions and the intended 95% bound construction really applied. The important distinction here is that “positive” means strictly above zero.
And if a switch with observed gap below 0.3 had a positive bound anyway?

That would not be ruled out by this hypothesis. Observed gap≥0.3 is a proposed sufficient-regime condition when combined with the others, not a stated necessary condition for every possible positive certificate. The hypothesis makes no negative prediction for a switch below that threshold.
Can we state the hypothesis once more without accidentally presenting it as a result?

The hypothesis is that, for supported-action switches in eight-stratum binary bandits with unit-bounded rewards, Γ≤1.25, switched-action propensity≥0.2, switch-mass≥0.1, and observed gap≥0.3 together yield a positive 95% lower gain bound when n≥20,000. Those are proposed sufficient conditions; their sufficiency and the validity of the bounds still need to be established.

To evaluate the proposed regime, let's simulate 10,000 confounded eight-stratum bandits with n=20,000, Γ=1.25, propensity≥0.2, switch-mass≥0.1, and gap≥0.3. We should measure true-gain coverage and positive-certification frequency. How should we describe that activity?

It is a proposed simulation evaluation, not a result. The activity calls for 10,000 confounded eight-stratum bandit simulations at n=20,000 and Γ=1.25, under the stated propensity, switch-mass, and gap thresholds. For each assessed switch, the two outcomes of interest are whether its gain bound covers the true policy gain and whether it certifies a strictly positive gain over the behavior policy. The activity specifies what to measure, but gives no measured values.
Are the 10,000 simulations and n=20,000 the same kind of count?

No. The 10,000 is the number of simulated bandits in the evaluation. The n=20,000 is the sample size specified for a bandit simulation. Keeping those counts distinct matters when describing the activity and its eventual measurements.
What do you mean by true-gain coverage in this evaluation?

For a lower gain bound, coverage asks whether the true gain over the behavior policy is at least as large as that lower bound. True-gain coverage is the frequency of that event across the simulated evaluations. It addresses the validity of the bound; it does not say how often the bound establishes improvement.
And positive-certification frequency is the frequency of what event?

It is the frequency with which the proposed 95% lower gain bound exceeds zero, so that the switch receives a certificate of strictly positive gain over the behavior policy. A bound that equals zero does not count as a positive certificate. This frequency measures how often the certificate is informative enough to establish improvement, separately from whether it covers the true gain.
If the true gain is positive, should that automatically count as a positive certification?

No. Positive certification is determined by the certificate: its lower gain bound must be strictly above zero. A switch can have a positive true gain while its lower bound remains at or below zero. The simulation can distinguish those situations because it measures true-gain coverage and positive-certification frequency separately.
Why measure both outcomes instead of just the fraction of bounds above zero?

Bounds above zero would tell us how often the proposed rule declares improvement, but not whether the bounds reliably cover the true gains. Conversely, coverage alone would not tell us whether the bounds ever clear zero. Measuring both speaks to the two aims behind the certificates: validity under the stated confounding bound and the ability to certify positive gains in the specified regime.
Does Γ=1.25 mean we are varying Γ up to 1.25 in this activity?

The activity specifies Γ=1.25 for the simulation evaluation. It does not describe a sweep over Γ values, so I would not add one. Nor does stating Γ=1.25 by itself specify every detail of how confounding is generated; it identifies the sensitivity-bound value for this evaluation.
Should I call the propensity threshold switched-action propensity≥0.2?

That is the precise term used for the overlap condition in the hypothesis being evaluated. Saying “switched-action propensity≥0.2” avoids making the condition sound like full action coverage. The activity also retains the separate switch-mass≥0.1 condition; neither threshold should be substituted for the other.
The activity says gap≥0.3. Is that a guaranteed true gain of at least 0.3?

No. In the proposed regime, the gap threshold concerns the observed gap. It must not be converted into a claim that the true policy gain, or the robust lower gain bound, is at least 0.3. The point of the evaluation is to see how the gain bounds behave under the stated conditions, including whether they cover true gains and whether they exceed zero.
Does the activity say that all 10,000 lower bounds will be positive?

No. That would be an outcome claim, and the activity supplies no outcomes. It asks us to measure positive-certification frequency across 10,000 simulations. That measurement would show how often positivity occurs in the evaluated setting, rather than assuming it happens in every simulation.
Could we report coverage as 95% now because these are called 95% lower bounds?

No. The 95% designation is the intended coverage level of the lower bounds. True-gain coverage is something this activity proposes to measure. We cannot replace the measurement with the nominal label or claim an observed coverage percentage before the simulations have been evaluated.
How does this simulation relate to the question about overlap and reward-gap conditions?

It evaluates one specified combination: propensity≥0.2, switch-mass≥0.1, and gap≥0.3 in confounded eight-stratum bandits at n=20,000 and Γ=1.25. Recording coverage and positive-certification frequency would make it possible to examine the behavior of the proposed bounds in that regime. The activity does not, by itself, identify thresholds for other regimes or establish a general sufficient condition.
Would measuring a high positive-certification frequency alone establish that the certificates remain valid under hidden confounding?

No. Positive-certification frequency measures how often a lower bound clears zero, not whether it covers the true gain. The true-gain coverage measurement is needed to assess that validity aspect in the simulated confounded bandits. Neither measurement should be inferred from the other.
And would the coverage measured over 10,000 simulations be a proof of coverage for every bandit covered by the Γ bound?

No. It would be an empirical coverage measurement for the simulated setting. It can assess how the proposed bounds behave in those 10,000 confounded eight-stratum bandits, but the activity alone does not prove a coverage guarantee across every setting allowed by a Γ-odds bound.
Can you state the activity concisely, keeping the thresholds and the two measurements distinct?

Simulate 10,000 confounded eight-stratum bandits at n=20,000 and Γ=1.25, with switched-action propensity≥0.2, switch-mass≥0.1, and observed gap≥0.3. Measure both the frequency with which the lower gain bounds cover the true policy gains and the frequency with which those bounds exceed zero and certify positive gains over the behavior policy. Those are measurements to perform, not results already obtained.
What did the evaluation report across the 10,000 eight-stratum bandits meeting the hypothesized thresholds at n=20,000?

True-gain coverage was 95.4%, and every lower gain bound was positive. Those are the two reported observations: how often the bounds covered the true policy gains, and whether the bounds cleared zero in the evaluated bandits.
What does 95.4% true-gain coverage mean here?

It means that, in 95.4% of the reported assessments, the lower bound covered the true gain: the true gain was at least as large as the lower bound. It is an empirical coverage measurement for these 10,000 bandits, not a statement about the size of the gains.
And how should I read “every lower bound was positive”?

Each assessed lower bound was strictly above zero, rather than equal to or below zero. Under the proposed certification rule, every assessed bound therefore issued a positive-gain certificate relative to the behavior policy. The statement reports the sign of every bound, not their individual values.
Can I describe the positive-certification frequency as 100%?

Yes, for the lower bounds assessed in this evaluation: every one was positive, so the observed positive-certification frequency among those bounds was 100%. Keep that tied to the evaluated bandits rather than presenting it as a guarantee for future or different bandits.
If every lower bound was positive, doesn't that also mean every bound covered the true gain?

No. Positivity and coverage are separate properties. A bound is positive when it exceeds zero; it covers when the true gain is at least as large as the bound. The results report positive bounds throughout the evaluation and true-gain coverage of 95.4%, so positivity did not imply coverage in every assessment.
Does a failure to cover necessarily mean the true gain was negative?

No. With a positive lower bound, a coverage failure means the true gain was below that bound. The true gain could still have been positive. The reported aggregate coverage does not tell us the signs or values of the true gains in the assessments where coverage failed.
Then can we say all 10,000 true policy gains were strictly positive?

Not from these two observations alone. Every lower bound being positive tells us that every assessed certificate declared a positive gain. Because coverage was not universal, that does not establish the sign of every underlying true gain. The results give an aggregate coverage percentage, not a list of true gains.
Does the 95.4% figure describe the chance that an individual positive certificate is correct?

It describes observed true-gain coverage across this evaluation. It should not be recast as a probability assigned to any particular certificate. An individual bound either covered its true gain or did not; the 95.4% figure aggregates those outcomes across the assessed bandits.
Remind me what “meeting the hypothesized thresholds” identifies in this setting.

It identifies the bandits as falling under the specified evaluation conditions: n=20,000 and the previously stated Γ=1.25, switched-action propensity≥0.2, switch-mass≥0.1, and observed gap≥0.3 conditions. Those conditions describe the evaluated setting; the reported observations are the 95.4% true-gain coverage and positive lower bounds throughout it.
Does the observed gap≥0.3 tell us that the positive lower bounds were all at least 0.3?

No. The observed-gap threshold and the lower gain bounds are different quantities. The result says each lower bound exceeded zero, but supplies no minimum value for those bounds beyond strict positivity. It also does not say that every true gain was at least 0.3.
Is n=20,000 the total across all 10,000 bandits?

No. The evaluation describes 10,000 bandits at n=20,000. The former is the number of simulated bandits; the latter is the sample size specified for a bandit. The coverage percentage summarizes assessments across that evaluation.
Can we infer how far above zero the bounds tended to be?

No. “Every lower bound was positive” gives their sign but not their magnitudes or distribution. A bound just above zero and a much larger positive bound both satisfy that description. No summary of the distances above zero is reported.
Does 95.4% coverage establish coverage separately in every stratum?

No. It is the reported aggregate true-gain coverage across the evaluated eight-stratum bandits. There is no stratum-specific coverage result in this evidence, so the aggregate percentage should not be assigned to each stratum separately.
What about switches exactly at the propensity or switch-mass thresholds—do we know their separate results?

Why does intersecting two 97.5% intervals give a 95% coverage claim?

The true gain belongs to the intersection precisely when it belongs to both intervals.
